newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. sergeant in Germany handed two year jail term.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sergeant in Germany handed two year jail term.

text.p: A U.S. military jury in Germany acquitted an army sergeant on Thursday of rape and sodomy charges against four female soldiers, but sentenced him to two years in prison after convicting him on lesser charges.

Sergeant First Class Julius Davis, 37, of Fayetteville, North Carolina, was found guilty on four counts each of indecent assault and maltreatment and one count each of fraternisation, obstruction of justice and disobeying an order.

The five-member all-male jury also gave Davis a dishonourable discharge but cleared him of six rape charges, one count of sodomy and other assault charges brought forward by 15 current or former female soldiers.
Prosecutors had asked for a minimum sentence of five years for Davies, who they called a "sexual predator" who used his rank to get sex.
An angry Davies told journalists after the sentencing that he felt betrayed by the army and also by U.S. civil rights leaders, whom he had appealed to for help in the case.
"Race was indeed an issue. I tried to contact the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People). They should have been here in my corner," Davies said.

"This was a witch hunt by the army. They corralled together these women to lie about me and then they laughed at me as the verdict was read. You can knock me down, but you can't knock me out. I am going to continue on with the rest of my life."

Defence attorneys did not mention race as a possible motivation for the charges against Davis, as had been claimed in another army sex scandal. But they selected the panel of jurors on the basis of their views on interracial dating.
Davis is black, while all of the women who made allegations against him were white or Hispanic.
Davis is the first soldier to be convicted outside the United States as part of the recent series of sex abuse scandals that have tainted the American armed forces.
Three sergeants at the Aberdeen Proving Ground base in Maryland have so far been convicted on rape and harassment charges, including one soldier who was given 25 years in jail.
Prosecutors did not bring forward any physical evidence of rape against Davis and defence attorneys argued the 15 women who made the allegations did so after being pressured by investigators.

Davis' lawyers also said the four women who claimed to have been raped had engaged in consensual sex and were motivated by revenge or were embarrassed by investigators who approached them to confront them about their role in possibly illegal activity.

Davis, a 17-year veteran, told jurors before his sentencing that he accepted responsibility for his actions and apologised to three of the victims in the courtroom, saying, "I hope you will forgive me for the humiliation that I have caused you."

His brother, Richard Davis, a chief petty officer aboard the U.S. Navy's U.S. Enterprise, told jurors his brother should be given a lenient sentence because he had been a "role model" for him and that they came from a poor background.
One of the witnesses, who told the court Davis sexually harassed her while in Bosnia, said she accepted the verdict.
"I have to accept the verdict of the jury even though I may not accept it," Specialist Brenda Hays told reporters.

Davis is one of three sergeants accused of sex-related crimes at the base where soldiers attend an orientation programme after arriving in Germany for duty. The centre's commander, who is a man, has been replaced by a woman.
One of the other soldiers, Sergeant First Class Paul Fuller, 26, of Columbus, Ohio, is to stand trial next week.
The army launched its probe against Davis after a former female soldier living in Nebraska called a military hotline last fall to allege that Davis he had raped her in 1993.

The sex scandal has also spread to the military's Pentagon headquarters in Washington where the army's top enlisted soldier, Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney, was put on forced leave after female soldiers made harassment allegations.
